summary:
Cesar operates under Colombia's national legal framework, and no Cesar-specific finding on trans law, enforcement practice or incidents is available for this department. The rules a trans visitor therefore faces in Cesar are the national ones, which are among the more developed in the region on paper and considerably weaker in application.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises recognition without a surgical requirement, and since a rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government identification has been changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended that change described the examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. The markers available on Colombian birth certificates and identity documents are F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero), with trans and non-binary markers carried on national identification from November 2025 and three gender options (male, female, X) on passports issued within Colombia since August 2023. These routes apply equally in Cesar, and no surgery or court ruling stands between a visitor and correct documents.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, same-sex marriage has been available since the national court's April 2016 ruling, same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015, and trans people have served openly in the armed forces since 2015. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The enforcement gap is severe and is the operative risk. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of that year. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising. An activist quoted in a July 2024 investigation stated that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people follows two distinct patterns in Colombia, and a visitor should not assume either is absent from Cesar. The first is armed-group activity in territories under their control. In Caquetá, armed groups ran social cleansing campaigns announced through flyers targeting drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots, and threatened a further wave; they gave the trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed, and she was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men. A friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". These are two departments out of many, illustrative of a nationwide armed-group threat rather than a local Cesar finding.

The second pattern is targeted killing in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated that they killed her for being who she was, President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. The CNN coverage of 6 August 2025 records the wider wave of attacks on LGBTQ+ people that followed. National totals give a sense of scale: 41 trans women were killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern. Courts have also intervened directly in detention, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
localsOnly:
For residents, Decree 0732 of 2026, signed on 9 July 2026 by the outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo, obliges public notaries to complete a gender-marker request within five business days, makes the first request free of charge, including a simultaneous name change, and shields the change history from public disclosure. The process itself is notarial and bureaucratic: no surgery, psychiatric evaluation or court ruling is required, and it applies in Cesar exactly as it does elsewhere in the country.

The Constitutional Court's ruling of 4 February 2022 ordered the government to offer the non-binary (NB) option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws. Compliance has been uneven at the counter: a 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS, documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Residents in Caquetá reported few options beyond sex work, and residents of armed-group-affected territories face displacement on top of that economic squeeze.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced data covers enforcement inside Cesar itself: whether notaries in the department process marker requests within the five-day window, whether refusals reported in the 2016 national study recur there, and whether any hate-crime prosecutions, detention protections or incidents have been recorded in the department. This is unresolved rather than absent, and should not be read as an assurance that practice matches statute.

The transfemicide point is likewise unresolved for Cesar. The finding that the prosecutor's office does not recognise the term comes from an activist quoted about another department's cases, and the killing totals cited are national figures; whether prosecutors in Cesar record trans killings as ordinary homicides or as a distinct category is not sourced here.

The status of the comprehensive trans law after 2025, and the implementation record of Decree 0732 of 2026 outside the main urban centres, are also unsourced for this department.
